hints: Look carefully at what changes exactly at 1 minute on the time axis and compare the gradient in phase A with phase B - what does a steeper fall in oxygen concentration tell you about rate of use?
Think about why mitochondria could only respire very slowly when they had pyruvate and Pi but no added ADP - what molecule cannot be made without ADP?
Link rapid ATP production to the electron transport chain - why must oxygen be used up faster when electrons are flowing faster?
walkthrough:
Reading the Graph as Rate of Oxygen Uptake**
A steeper downward slope means oxygen concentration is falling faster, so oxygen is being taken up and used faster. In phase A only pyruvate and Pi are present, so only a very slow background rate of respiration is possible.

Why ADP Switches On Fast Respiration**
ADP + Pi are the raw materials for making ATP in oxidative phosphorylation on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Without ADP, ATP synthase cannot work and the whole electron transport chain backs up. Adding ADP at 1 minute removes this block, so electrons flow rapidly and ATP is made rapidly.

Why Oxygen Use Must Increase**
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor at the end of the electron transport chain, combining with electrons and protons to form water. When electron flow and oxidative phosphorylation speed up, much more oxygen is reduced per minute, so the oxygen concentration in the buffer falls steeply in phase B.
Final answer: Faster rate of aerobic respiration in phase B. ADP added allows ATP synthesis by oxidative phosphorylation, so oxygen is used faster as the final electron acceptor.

hints: A levelling out means oxygen is no longer being used up quickly - think about which of the added substances added at 0 and 1 minute could now have been used up.
walkthrough:
Levelling Means Something Ran Out**
In phase C the line is almost flat, so very little oxygen is being removed. That tells you aerobic respiration has almost stopped, not because the mitochondria are dead but because one substrate has been used up. This could be the ADP added at 1 minute, or Pi, pyruvate or even dissolved oxygen itself becoming limiting.
Final answer: ADP / Pi / oxygen / pyruvate becomes limiting / runs out, so respiration slows / stops.

hints: Start with the problem for the roots - how does diffusion of oxygen in water compare with diffusion in air, and what does that mean for aerobic respiration?
Think about the special air-space tissue found in stems and roots of water plants and how it could connect leaves in the air to roots underwater.
Consider what other way leaves might help get oxygen to submerged parts, for example trapping bubbles of air.
If oxygen still cannot reach root cells, what type of respiration must they use and what toxic product builds up in plant cells?
Think about two ways rice root cells cope with that toxic product - tolerating it or breaking it down - plus how they still get enough ATP without oxygen.
walkthrough:
The Problem of Submerged Roots**
Oxygen diffuses very slowly in water and waterlogged mud is very low in oxygen. Root cells need ATP for active uptake of ions and growth, so they struggle to carry out enough aerobic respiration.

Aerenchyma as an Internal Airway**
Rice stems and roots contain aerenchyma, tissue with large interconnected air spaces. Oxygen from leaves and stems in the air can diffuse down through these continuous gas channels directly to the submerged root cells.

Keeping Aerobic Respiration Going**
That delivered oxygen allows root mitochondria to continue aerobic respiration with a high ATP yield. Ridges on some leaves also trap a film of air when underwater, helping gas exchange to continue.

Coping When Anaerobic Respiration Is Forced**
Where oxygen still runs out, root cells switch to anaerobic respiration, producing ethanol by alcoholic fermentation. Ethanol is toxic, but rice root cells can tolerate it.

Detoxifying and Maintaining ATP Supply**
Root cells produce alcohol dehydrogenase / ethanol dehydrogenase to break down ethanol. Some rice varieties also have a high rate of anaerobic respiration so that, despite only 2 ATP per glucose, enough ATP is generated to survive waterlogging.

Final answer: Low oxygen concentration in water / waterlogged soil. Aerenchyma provides large air spaces for diffusion of oxygen / gases down to root cells for aerobic respiration. Leaves trap air underwater. Under anaerobic conditions roots carry out alcoholic fermentation producing ethanol, which root cells tolerate and break down using alcohol / ethanol dehydrogenase. Some varieties maintain a high anaerobic respiration rate to generate more ATP.
